questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in bold: "The chairman's assessment of the project was refreshingly **candid**."
questions.explanation: *Candid* means open and honest in what one says, so *frank* matches it exactly. The word *refreshingly* is a clue: it signals approval, which rules out any negative synonym.

distractorRationale.b: Honesty can be blunt, but *rude* adds deliberate offence, which *candid* does not carry
distractorRationale.c: Refers to how long the assessment was, not to how honest it was
distractorRationale.d: *Evasive* is the opposite — it means avoiding the truth

questions.stem: Choose the option most nearly opposite in meaning to the word in bold: "Rainfall was **abundant** throughout the planting season."
questions.explanation: *Abundant* means present in large quantity, so its opposite is *scarce*, meaning available only in small quantity. Antonym questions punish speed-reading, because the most attractive option is often a synonym rather than an opposite.

distractorRationale.a: *Plentiful* is a synonym of *abundant*, not an antonym — the classic trap in this question type
distractorRationale.c: *Steady* describes the pattern of the rainfall, not the amount
distractorRationale.d: *Seasonal* describes when the rain fell, which is unrelated to quantity

questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in bold: "Considering his age, the magistrate imposed a **lenient** sentence."
questions.explanation: *Lenient* means not severe in punishment, so *mild* is the closest match. The phrase *considering his age* points the same way: it explains why the magistrate showed mercy.

distractorRationale.c: A long sentence would be severe, which contradicts *lenient*
distractorRationale.d: Mercy is not the same as injustice; the sentence implies the decision was reasonable

questions.stem: Choose the option most nearly opposite in meaning to the word in bold: "The inspector **commended** the staff for their punctuality."
questions.explanation: *Commend* means to praise formally, so its opposite is *condemn*, meaning to express strong disapproval. Be careful not to confuse *commend* with the similar-looking *command*, which means to order.

distractorRationale.a: *Praised* is a synonym, not an opposite
distractorRationale.b: *Rewarded* is a related positive action rather than an opposite
distractorRationale.d: *Observed* is neutral and expresses no judgement at all

questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in bold: "The clerk kept **meticulous** records of every transaction."
questions.explanation: *Meticulous* means showing great attention to small details, which is exactly what *painstaking* describes. The word says nothing about how many records there were or who could see them.

distractorRationale.b: *Confidential* concerns secrecy, a different idea entirely
distractorRationale.c: *Hurried* work is the opposite of careful attention to detail
distractorRationale.d: *Voluminous* refers to bulk, and careful records may be brief

questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in bold as it is used here: "The guards on duty at the gate were **relieved** at six o'clock in the morning."
questions.explanation: *Relieve* has two common senses: to ease somebody's distress, and to take over somebody's duty. The words *on duty at the gate* and *at six o'clock* point to a change of shift, so the second sense applies. Always let the context, not the commoner meaning, decide.

distractorRationale.a: This is the commoner sense of the word, but nothing in the sentence suggests the guards were distressed
distractorRationale.c: Confuses *relieved* with the adjective meaning glad, which needs no time reference
distractorRationale.d: Being relieved of duty for a shift is very different from losing one's job

questions.stem: Choose the option most nearly opposite in meaning to the word in bold: "The new administration promised a **transparent** procurement process."
questions.explanation: In the language of governance, *transparent* means conducted openly so that the public can see what is happening. Its opposite is therefore *secretive*, meaning deliberately hidden from view.

distractorRationale.a: *Open* is a synonym rather than an opposite
distractorRationale.c: Cost is a separate matter from openness
distractorRationale.d: A process can be efficient and secretive at the same time, so this is unrelated

questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in bold: "Parents protested against the **exorbitant** school fees."
questions.explanation: *Exorbitant* describes a price far higher than is reasonable, so *excessive* is the closest match. The fact that the parents protested supports this reading.

distractorRationale.b: Fees may be compulsory without being unreasonably high
distractorRationale.c: A sudden increase might cause protest, but *exorbitant* refers to the amount rather than the timing
distractorRationale.d: *Moderate* is the opposite of the intended sense

questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in bold: "Fame in the entertainment industry can be **ephemeral**."
questions.explanation: *Ephemeral* means lasting for a very short time, so *short-lived* is the correct match. The root is the Greek *hemera*, meaning day — literally something that lasts only a day.

distractorRationale.c: Confuses *ephemeral* with *ethereal*, which suggests something delicate or otherworldly
distractorRationale.d: Refers to profit rather than duration

questions.stem: Because *slim* and *skinny* are synonyms, either word may be used in any sentence without changing the effect on the reader.
questions.explanation: False. Synonyms share a core meaning but differ in connotation — the feelings they carry. *Slim* is complimentary while *skinny* is critical, so "she looked slim in the dress" and "she looked skinny in the dress" say very different things about the speaker's attitude. Always test a synonym against the tone of the sentence.
